got_right: Pre-registered with documented amendments (assignment algorithm, Lin covariate adjustment), so the 32-arm comparison against one control is confirmatory, not post hoc.
Unusually broad stimulus set (videos, text, images, memes, many student-made) tested in one pool with a shared control (mean trust 3.69, n=664), which allows direct comparison of message formats.
Lin-adjusted, inverse-probability-weighted models with HC2 errors respect the adaptive assignment and gain precision from pre-treatment trust.

The strongest result, the 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video lowering trust by 0.17 (95% CI [-0.26,-0.08], p=0.0002), is a clear backfire signal that survives scrutiny better than the small positives.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: Adaptive assignment left most arms near 120-180 respondents, so per-arm intervals are about ±0.15 and cannot detect effects of the size seen (0.06). Three of the five 'significant' arms are small positives whose intervals almost reach zero.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: Arm n of 116-180 for most arms versus 853-921 for videos 15 and 20; Video 12 CI [0.005, 0.123], p=0.034.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: Thirty-two uncorrected two-sided tests were run. Only the 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video clearly survives a Bonferroni threshold (0.05/32≈0.0016). The other four, p of 0.009 to 0.034, are consistent with chance.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: Five of 32 arms at p<0.05 against about 1.6 expected under the null; p=0.0002, 0.0093, 0.0104, 0.0116, 0.0341.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: Each arm bundles content, format, length and source, and several student videos have no recorded title. Even a real effect cannot be attributed to any feature of the message.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: Video 12, Video 15 and Student-made video (20) are untitled or minimally described uploads.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: Trust is measured once, immediately after exposure, on a 5-point scale, and the single-item check shows almost no signal. The effects are small relative to the scale and durability is unknown.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: Control mean 3.685; positive effects about 0.06; the single-item outcome has only one visible arm (Video 12, p=0.048).

why_it_did_not_land.detail: The pipeline's completers robustness check reused the same 7,803 rows as the main model, so it supplies no robustness evidence. Modelling used 7,803 of 8,572 analysed rows.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: E1 shows orig_n = compl_n = 7803 with identical estimates; the checking agent's correction says the same.

briefs.title: Decomposing the 'trust science too much' backfire
briefs.question: Which feature of the 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video (its fallibility framing, its format, or its source) lowers trust in science?
briefs.why_this_fixes_the_failure: Addresses the design and power causes: it replaces bundled stimuli with a manipulated mechanism and concentrates sample on the one robust effect.
briefs.design_sketch: Randomise respondents to the original video, a text transcript of it, a version without the fallibility segment, a matched-length neutral video, and a pure control. Outcome is the same 5-point trust measure, with pre-treatment trust as a covariate and a delayed re-measure after about one week. Sample is US adults from an online panel, with the same exclusions as the original.

power_target.basis: Observed effect of -0.17 for the video; the pooled SD implied by the SEs is about 0.9. The ~0.12 MDE allows for shrinkage of the original estimate, and the power table gives no contrasts.

briefs.title: Do the small positive videos replicate across samples and baseline trust?
briefs.question: Do the three small positive video effects (about +0.06) replicate in a fresh sample, and do they differ by baseline trust or partisanship?
briefs.why_this_fixes_the_failure: Addresses the multiplicity and sample causes: a confirmatory replication of the three positive arms with a single correction, plus a test of where the effect holds.
briefs.design_sketch: Run videos 12, 15 and 20, the strongest-effect comparison video, and a control in a new panel, preferably a different vendor from Lucid. Pre-register three directional tests, with the interaction of arm and pre-treatment trust (low versus high) and of arm and party identification. Add a title and a content coding for each student video so features can be linked to effects.
briefs.moderator_or_condition: Baseline trust in science (low vs high) and party identification, across a different panel vendor.

power_target.basis: Observed +0.06 effects for videos 12, 15 and 20, with SD about 0.9; 80% power at alpha 0.05 needs roughly 3,500-4,400 per arm. A single contrast is not computed in the power table.

briefs.title: Archive stimuli and arm-level assignment data
briefs.question: Can the untitled student videos and the adaptive assignment log be documented well enough to attribute effects to content?
briefs.why_this_fixes_the_failure: Addresses the measurement and design causes: untitled stimuli cannot be interpreted or replicated.
briefs.design_sketch: Recover the files for videos 8, 10, 12, 15, 25 and 32. Have two coders rate each on length, tone, presence of an expert, and fallibility framing, using the TIDieR checklist. Publish the assignment probabilities by wave so inverse-probability weights can be audited.

verdict: A follow-up is worth running, but narrowly. Only the 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video backfire (-0.17, p=0.0002) is robust to multiplicity. The three +0.06 effects are fragile, and the pipeline's completers check added no evidence. The retrieved literature is reporting-standards material, so no live empirical debate is visible and none is invented. Run the backfire decomposition first, since it has the largest effect and an explicit mechanism. Then run the larger replication of the positive videos, with stimulus documentation (the data brief) done in parallel at little cost.
